claims.text: High Cr and Ta concentrations in certain refractory HEAs promote rapid formation and sustained adherence of a CrTaO4-based oxide layer at high temperature.
The CrTaO4-based layer acts as a self-healing barrier that prevents further oxygen ingress and retards oxidation.
The proposed initial refractory HEA has multiple principal elements, optimized Cr and Ta levels, and a homogeneous pre-oxidation microstructure.
A controlled comparison can vary Cr and Ta levels while keeping the other alloying elements and processing conditions identical.
Isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C for up to 200 hours is an applicable test condition for the proposed refractory HEA.
Microstructure and grain size should be held constant during the Cr/Ta comparison.
The relevant structural mediator is a continuous, dense CrTaO4-based surface layer.
Elevated Cr and Ta concentrations drive preferential oxidation to form CrTaO4.
The CrTaO4-based oxide adheres well to the alloy substrate.
The CrTaO4-based oxide limits oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
Continuous oxidation of the underlying alloy repairs minor damage in the oxide layer.
Lower-Cr/Ta variants fail to form or retain the protective CrTaO4-based layer and consequently oxidize more rapidly.
An optimized high-Cr/Ta alloy will show lower oxidation weight gain than an otherwise identical reduced-Cr/Ta control.
The optimized high-Cr/Ta alloy will develop a thinner and more uniform oxide layer than the reduced-Cr/Ta control.
The reduced-Cr/Ta control will develop a more porous or discontinuous oxide layer and exhibit higher mass gain.
At 1100 °C, formation of a protective CrTaO4-based layer is associated with parabolic oxidation behavior and low weight gain over 200 hours.
The hypothesis applies primarily near 1100 °C and during long-duration oxidation, while applicability at lower temperatures or shorter durations is uncertain.
The critical Cr and Ta concentrations and the effects of other alloying elements have not been quantified.
Failure of the high-Cr/Ta alloy to show a statistically significant reduction in weight gain and to form a continuous, dense CrTaO4-based layer relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
